title: Aristotle
note: Aristotle, Plato's student, placed form inside things: a substance is a compound of matter and form. He explained things by four causes and traced motion to an unmoved mover. In ethics, the human good is rational activity done well over a whole life, built by habits that hit the mean between extremes.

read.title: Form in things, virtue in habit
text: Aristotle studied with Plato for about twenty years, then built a different system. He agreed that knowledge needs stable forms, but he placed them inside the things we meet. This horse is a substance, a unity of matter and form. Its form is what makes it a horse, and its matter is what that form organizes.

To explain anything, Aristotle asked four questions. What is it made of? What is its form? What brought it about? What is it for? A house is bricks and wood, built on a plan, by a builder, for shelter. Nature too acts for ends, as roots grow down and leaves turn toward light.

His ethics follows the same pattern. Everything with a function does well when it performs that function excellently. The distinctive human function is to live by reason, so human flourishing, eudaimonia, is rational activity in accordance with virtue over a complete life. Ethical virtues such as courage are stable traits formed by practice, just as one becomes a builder by building. Each lies in a mean relative to the situation: the brave person fears what is truly dangerous, neither cowering nor charging recklessly. Practical wisdom finds that mean in each case.
